title: Impression Management
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore impression management, a concept developed by sociologist Erving Goffman (spelled "Irving" in the transcript; hosts also say Goffman). They cover Goffman's 1956 book The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, dramaturgical theory, front stage, backstage and off stage selves, face work, and how people handle embarrassing moments. They discuss Leary and Kowalski's model of impression motivation and impression construction (self concept, desired identity, target value, role constraints, current social image), the difference between impression management and masking in neurodivergent people, authenticity, stigma and code switching, and gender norms. The episode ends with a listener email about nixtamalization and a sign-off.
topics: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
Leary and Kowalski impression motivation and construction

entities.name: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Goffman
segments.summary: Hosts riff on front stage selves and the Rush song Limelight, then introduce impression management and sociologist Irving Goffman, who shifted sociology toward small everyday interactions.

segments.title: Goffman's background and neurodiversity
segments.summary: Hosts describe Goffman as a Canadian American sociologist whose work began in the 1950s, his empathy for marginalized people, and how social skill varies, including neurodivergent people and narcissism.

segments.title: Definitions of impression management
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh define impression management, self presentation and perception management, and note that everyone engages in it to some degree.

segments.title: Dramaturgical theory and social scripts
segments.summary: Goffman's 1956 book The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life and dramaturgical theory are introduced. People follow social scripts, and performance varies by setting. Hosts compare this to drama and comedy, where characters violate expectations.
topics: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life

segments.title: Common definition of the situation and elevator discomfort
segments.summary: Goffman's idea of a common definition of the situation is illustrated with a bus stop scene. Nonverbal cues are described as harder to fake, and the hosts discuss how norm violations unsettle people, using an elevator as an example.

segments.title: Front stage, backstage and off stage selves
segments.summary: Goffman's distinction between front stage, backstage and off stage selves is explained, with a teacher running into a student at the grocery store as an example of an off stage interaction.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Face work and saving face
segments.summary: Goffman's concept of face work is covered, including facial expressions that conflict with words and helping others save face. Hosts relate this to a personal anecdote about falling off a bike.

segments.title: Embarrassment after falling in public
segments.summary: Lucy McDonald's view that people look around after falling and say things like oops to reassure others is discussed, with a story about a college bike wreck and a fall in a parking lot.

segments.title: Civil inattention and ignoring others
segments.summary: Civil inattention as a Western norm is discussed. Hosts say phones have increased people ignoring each other, and Southern politeness is contrasted with that.

segments.title: Elevator experiments and Candid Camera
segments.summary: The apocryphal story of Goffman turning around in an elevator is discussed, along with a Candid Camera episode where a person joined the crowd facing the rear.

segments.title: Breaching experiments
segments.summary: Harold Garfinkel's breaching experiments are mentioned, in which people deliberately violated social norms, and the hosts note how these are pranks.

segments.title: Impression motivation and impression construction
segments.summary: Psychologists Mark Leary and Robin Kowalski's 1990 model is introduced, splitting impression management into motivation (relevance, goal value, perceived current image) and construction.

segments.title: Self concept, desired identity and target value
segments.summary: The first constructive components are described: self concept as a steamer trunk of props, desired identity, and target value, with caution about distancing from others and inauthenticity.

segments.title: Role constraints, current social image and other techniques
segments.summary: The remaining constructive elements are covered, including role constraints, current social image, flattery, conforming, emotional suppression, basking in reflected glory, and downward comparison.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Online identity, authenticity and self presentation
segments.summary: Online identity is raised as a topic for a separate episode. Schlenker's view that all social interaction involves self presentation is contrasted with self expression, and the hosts discuss Nathan Fielder's The Rehearsal.

segments.title: Automatic behavior and rehearsal
segments.summary: Automatic behavior is discussed as something learned through practice. Schlenker compares it to breathing, and performance can shift between high and low gear.

segments.title: Backstage anxiety and gender performance
segments.summary: The hosts joke about backstage anxiety and meet and greets, then discuss Judith Butler's view that gender is shaped by social forces and childhood experiences.

segments.title: Gender fluidity and social norm violation
segments.summary: Reaction to gender-fluid people is discussed as a conflict between authenticity and the comfort of others. The hosts note that social norms change only when violated, and reference Pleasantville.

segments.title: Stigma, discredited persons and code switching
segments.summary: Goffman's concept of stigma is described, including the discredited versus discreditable distinction. Code switching by African Americans is discussed as impression management, along with a personal story about a classmate's name.

segments.title: Masking and autism
segments.summary: Masking by autistic people is distinguished from general impression management, citing researchers Amy Pearson and Kieran Rose. The hosts recommend Love on the Spectrum.

segments.title: Listener mail: popcorn and nixtamalization
segments.summary: Listener Bob writes about a Good Eats segment on Montezuma's revenge, pellagra, and nixtamalization of maize after the popcorn episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask for listener email and sign off.
